title: Acid-Fast Staining (Ziehl-Neelsen)

references.label: Biosafety in Microbiological and Biomedical Laboratories (BMBL)

purpose: To identify organisms with a waxy, mycolic-acid-rich cell wall (notably Mycobacterium species) that do not reliably take up the Gram stain and instead require a stain that can penetrate and then resist decolorization by acid-alcohol.
principle: Mycolic acids in the cell wall of acid-fast organisms bind and retain carbolfuchsin (aided by heat or a phenol-based mordant) even when challenged with an acid-alcohol decolorizer that strips the stain from non-acid-fast cells. Acid-fast cells therefore remain red/pink after decolorization; non-acid-fast cells decolorize and take up the methylene blue counterstain instead.

procedure.instruction: Prepare a thin smear on a clean slide, air dry, and heat-fix.

Flood the smear with carbolfuchsin and heat gently to steaming (classic method) or allow extended contact time without heat (cold/Kinyoun-style modification), then hold for the method's specified time.
procedure.note: Heat and the phenol in carbolfuchsin both help drive the stain through the waxy cell wall; the two approaches (heat-based Ziehl-Neelsen vs. no-heat Kinyoun) are distinct standard methods, not interchangeable mid-procedure.

procedure.instruction: Decolorize with acid-alcohol until only faint pink runoff remains — this step, not the primary stain, is what actually distinguishes acid-fast from non-acid-fast cells.
procedure.note: Over-decolorization can strip even acid-fast organisms; under-decolorization leaves background debris falsely appearing acid-fast.

procedure.instruction: Counterstain with methylene blue, then rinse and blot dry.

observations: Acid-fast organisms appear red/pink (retained carbolfuchsin) against a blue background of non-acid-fast material and counterstained cells/debris.
interpretation: A positive (acid-fast) result narrows identification toward Mycobacterium and a small number of other partially acid-fast genera; it does not by itself identify species and is always interpreted alongside culture, growth characteristics, and (in a clinical setting) additional confirmatory testing.
criticalNotes: This is a distinct staining chemistry from Gram staining, not a variant of it — acid-fast organisms are typically reported as such rather than forced into a Gram-positive/negative call.
Smear preparation and handling for suspected Mycobacterium specimens carries its own biosafety considerations separate from the staining chemistry itself.
precautions: Treat all specimens as potentially infectious; specimens suspected of containing Mycobacterium tuberculosis require handling consistent with the institution's risk assessment and biosafety guidance, not just standard bench precautions.
Carbolfuchsin contains phenol — handle and dispose of per local chemical safety procedure.
Heat-based decolorization/staining steps require care around open flame and flammable reagents.
limitations: A negative acid-fast smear does not rule out mycobacterial infection — smear sensitivity is limited relative to culture or molecular methods.
Staining quality is technique-sensitive; inconsistent heating or decolorization time is a common source of false results.
biosafetyNotes: Biosafety level for handling a specimen or culture suspected of containing Mycobacterium tuberculosis is determined by institutional risk assessment (see BSL vs. Risk Group), not by the staining procedure itself — many institutions require enhanced precautions (e.g. a Class II BSC) well beyond what a routine Gram stain needs.
